label: Tehillim (Psalms) — Part 2 — Psalms 21–41
summary_plain: Psalms 21 through 41 move between royal victory psalms and deep personal lament. Psalm 22 opens with the cry: My El, my El, why have you forsaken me? The speaker is mocked, pierced, his garments divided by lot — yet the psalm ends not in death but in YHWH's deliverance and the declaration that all the ends of the earth shall turn to YHWH. Psalm 23 declares: YHWH is my shepherd, I shall not want. He leads me beside still waters, he restores my soul. Psalm 24 asks: Who shall ascend the hill of YHWH? He who has clean hands and a pure heart. Psalm 34 proclaims: YHWH is near to the brokenhearted. Psalm 37 counsels: do not fret because of evildoers — trust in YHWH and do good.
summary_scholarly: The ACR reads Psalms 21-41 from the Dead Sea Scrolls witnesses (fragments across 4QPsa-q, 11QPsa) and the Orit Ge'ez. Psalm 22 is critical to understanding the Great Eraser mechanism: the NT appropriates the opening line (My El, my El, why have you forsaken me) as a crucifixion quotation (Matthew 27:46), but the full psalm is a communal lament that resolves in national restoration — 'All the ends of the earth shall remember and turn to YHWH, and all the families of the nations shall worship before you' (22:27). The psalm was never about an individual dying for sins. The NT extracted one verse from its covenantal context and reframed it as prophecy fulfilled. The DSS preserve Psalm 22 as a communal lament of the covenant people under oppression — the suffering is national, the deliverance is YHWH's, and the resolution is that all nations acknowledge YHWH directly.

key_terms.definition: A Zion psalm of refuge: YHWH is a present help in trouble; the earth may change and mountains fall into the sea, but YHWH of Hosts is with the community. 'Be still and know that I am YHWH' (46:10).

key_terms.term: Psalm 51 Create in Me a Clean Heart
key_terms.definition: David's great penitential psalm — attributed to the occasion after Natan confronted him. Contains the deepest covenant repentance language: 'Create in me a clean heart, O YHWH, and renew a right spirit within me.'
'The sacrifices of YHWH are a broken spirit; a broken and contrite heart, O YHWH, you will not despise.' YHWH values genuine repentance over ritual offering.

Opens with Moshe's wilderness cry from Bamidbar 10:35: 'Let YHWH arise, let his enemies be scattered.' The psalm celebrates YHWH's march from the Kushite south through the wilderness and enthronement on Mount Tzion.

'Nobles shall come from Mitzrayim; Kush shall hasten to stretch out her hands to YHWH.' This psalm affirms that the Kushite and Mitzrayim peoples will come and honor YHWH — the covenant is not ethnically restricted to one group.

key_terms.term: Psalm 72 Royal Psalm for the Poor
key_terms.definition: A royal psalm attributed to Shlomo — prayer for the king who will defend the poor, deliver the needy, and crush the oppressor. 'May he defend the poor of the people, give deliverance to the children of the needy, and crush the oppressor' (72:4).

A psalm superscription type — 13 psalms are labeled 'maskil,' possibly meaning a contemplative or instructive composition, or a poem requiring skillful performance. Its exact technical meaning is uncertain.
A rare superscription type appearing in Psalm 7; its meaning is uncertain — possibly a lament or crying song, or a composition of varying emotional intensity. Also appears in Havaqquq 3:1.

A superscription type found in Psalms 16, 56–60; its meaning is uncertain — possibly related to 'gold' suggesting a poem of special value, or a word of uncertain Akkadian or Aramaic origin indicating a specific genre.

Appears in Psalm 22's superscription ('according to the Doe of the Dawn') — a musical direction indicating a specific tune or instrument. Also related to the verb meaning 'to afflict/humble,' giving the word liturgical overtones for Yom Kippur use.

faq.question: What is the spiritual crisis at the heart of Psalm 42–43?
faq.answer: Psalms 42–43 (originally one psalm) express the crisis of a Levite separated from YHWH's Temple, mocked by enemies asking 'Where is your Creator?' The refrain repeats three times: 'Why are you cast down, O my soul? Hope in YHWH; for I shall again praise him.' The psalm models holding onto covenant trust even when the felt experience is desolation.

faq.question: What is the message of Psalm 46 and why is 'Be still' important?
faq.answer: Psalm 46 is a song of absolute confidence in YHWH's protection even when the earth shakes and kingdoms fall. 'Be still and know that I am YHWH' is not a command to passive silence — the Hebrew word means to let go of striving and contention, to cease from one's own anxious activity. The 'knowing' follows from the stillness: when you stop grasping, you recognize who YHWH is.

faq.question: What makes Psalm 51 the premier penitential psalm?
faq.answer: Psalm 51 moves through the complete arc of genuine repentance: acknowledgment of sin (vv.1-5), appeal to YHWH's covenant loyalty and compassion (v.1), request for inner transformation (vv.10-12), commitment to restored worship (vv.13-17), and the recognition that YHWH values a broken and contrite heart over ritual sacrifice alone. It became the liturgical standard for communal confession.

faq.question: Why does Psalm 51:4 say 'against you alone have I sinned' when David wronged Uriyah?
faq.answer: The statement acknowledges that all sin is ultimately a violation of YHWH's covenant standards. While Uriyah was wronged (and Batsheva, and the people), the fundamental wrong is against YHWH's Torah. The 'alone' also expresses the theological reality that only YHWH has the authority to judge and forgive at the deepest level — human courts can punish but cannot restore the covenant relationship.

faq.question: What is Psalm 68 and why is the Kush reference significant?
faq.answer: Psalm 68 is a great processional hymn celebrating YHWH's march from the wilderness to Mount Tzion. It describes YHWH coming from the south — from the region of Sinai, Teiman, Bashan — in the tradition of Devarim 33 and Shofetim 5. Verse 31 specifically names Mitzrayim and Kush as peoples who will hasten to honor YHWH. This is the Hebrew psalm corpus confirming that YHWH's covenant community and worship include the Kushite peoples.

faq.question: What does Psalm 72 pray for the king and why is justice for the poor central?
faq.answer: Psalm 72 sets the standard for covenant kingship: the king who fulfills his role defends the poor, delivers the needy, and crushes the oppressor. The prayer is not for the king's military glory or wealth but for the king's just governance of the vulnerable. This is the Hebrew royal ideal — power measured by protection of the least powerful. YHWH's kingship embodies this same standard.

faq.question: What is a Maskil psalm and why are they significant?
faq.answer: Thirteen psalms carry the superscription 'Maskil' — a word possibly meaning a contemplative, instructive, or skillfully crafted composition. These include Psalms 32, 42, 44, 45, 52-55, 74, 78, 88, 89, and 142. They tend to be reflective and intellectually engaged rather than straightforward praise or lament. The exact performance or liturgical distinction they signal is uncertain.

faq.question: How does Psalm 46 respond to the experience of cosmic chaos?
faq.answer: Psalm 46 deliberately uses the most extreme chaos imagery — mountains falling into the sea, waters roaring and foaming, the earth tottering — and declares that even in the midst of this, YHWH is a present refuge. The city of YHWH (Tzion) has a river that gladdens it; YHWH is in its midst and will not be moved. The confidence is not denial of the chaos but trust in YHWH's presence within it.

faq.question: What does Psalm 51:10's request for a 'clean heart' imply about inner transformation?
faq.answer: The word 'create' (bara) in 'create in me a clean heart' is the same word used for YHWH's creation of the heavens and earth in Bereshit 1. It is exclusively used of divine action — humans cannot bara, only YHWH can. The psalmist is acknowledging that inner transformation is YHWH's work, not human resolve. The request is for a creative act — a new inner reality that the person cannot manufacture by willpower.

faq.question: Why does Psalm 68 describe YHWH marching from the south?
faq.answer: The ancient Hebrew memory consistently associated YHWH's presence with the south — Sinai, Teiman, Paran, the wilderness regions tied to the Exodus and covenant formation. This southward orientation in YHWH's march (Ps.68, Devarim 33, Shofetim 5, Havaqquq 3) reflects the actual geography of the covenant community's origin story: out of Mitzrayim and through the southern wilderness regions of Kush and Sinai.
